text: A smart contract by itself is useless to a normal user — nobody calls it by hand from a command line. Everything a user touches, and everything a developer uses to build, test, and operate around that contract, is written in JavaScript or its typed sibling, TypeScript.

JavaScript shows up in three places in every real dApp. The frontend — the page a user interacts with, including the Connect Wallet button, almost always React or Next.js. The libraries that talk to the chain — ethers.js and viem. And backend scripts — Node.js code that deploys contracts, indexes events, or runs a bot.

It's tempting to skip straight to connecting a wallet and calling a contract, but that's just JavaScript syntax wrapped around a library call. If const, arrow functions, async/await, and array methods aren't second nature yet, every tutorial becomes fighting two unfamiliar things at once.

Two chapters of JavaScript, then async JavaScript, then TypeScript, then Node.js, ending in a capstone script that reads real blockchain data. Next up: getting your dev environment installed — Node.js and VS Code.
